guide.text: The sources are October 21, 2026 board notes and the FY2026 annual report of Quillmere Rolling Library, a fictional bookmobile nonprofit.
The group made 281 of 292 stops, and its 2009 vehicle caused all 11 missed stops.
Route Eighteen would add a second van to reach four north-county schools with 310 students, at a total cost of $148,000.
The county's $40,000 is committed, the $85,000 ask to Beaumont-Tully is pending, and a $23,000 donor campaign is planned.
Third-grade reading rose from 41 percent to 49 percent at six schools, but state tutors worked in four of them, so the library does not claim the gain.

plain_draft:
Slide 1: Route Eighteen: One Aging Bookmobile, 310 Students Waiting
Quillmere Rolling Library | Beaumont-Tully Rural Literacy Fund review, December 4, 2026
We missed 11 of 292 scheduled stops in FY2026, and our 2009 bookmobile caused every one
The vehicle passed 214,000 miles this spring
October: lost a transmission line. February: failed its brake inspection. June: overheated twice
When we miss a school stop, that class goes four weeks between visits instead of two
Four north-county schools have asked to join: Dunmore, Pike Hollow, Sayer Flat, East Kettle
Together they have 310 K-6 students and no school librarian
We cannot add them with one aging vehicle that already misses stops

Slide 2: Who We Serve and What We Did in FY2026
A two-person bookmobile serving rural Corrow County elementary schools that have no school librarian and are more than 25 miles from a public library branch
14 schools, 1,180 K-6 students, a visit every other week for 36 weeks
281 of 292 stops completed (96%)
21,460 items checked out, up from 18,930 in FY2025
About 4,100 of those checkouts came from new classroom crate loans, used by 52 of 61 teachers
91% return rate | 846 new county library cards for students
214 children enrolled in summer reading; 131 reached the eight-book goal

Slide 3: What Teachers See
"Bookmobile Tuesday is the only day the whole class runs to the window. When you missed in February, three kids asked me if you were coming back."
Dorrie Akin, third-grade teacher, Fallow Creek Elementary (quoted with permission)
Vehicle costs went from $19,700 in FY2025 to $31,900 in FY2026, and nearly all of the increase was repairs

Slide 4: Third-Grade Reading: What We Know and What We Don't
6 of our 14 schools shared spring third-grade reading benchmark results (188 students)
At those six schools, third graders reading at or above grade level went from 41% (spring 2025) to 49% (spring 2026)
That same year, state-funded reading tutors worked in four of those six schools
We cannot separate our effect from the tutors' effect, and we do not claim this gain as ours
Other limits: we have no comparison group, and the schools that agreed to share data may be the ones with the most engaged principals
What we can say: the schools where children read the most books from our shelves were also the schools where scores rose
Next year: we will ask all 14 schools for data and track checkouts per student

Slide 5: The Plan: Route Eighteen
Buy a used high-roof cargo van, refit it with shelving and a wheelchair lift, and run it on a new north route
Add Dunmore, Pike Hollow, Sayer Flat and East Kettle
The 2009 bookmobile moves to the shorter southern route and stays in service through FY2028 while we save to replace it
With two vehicles, a breakdown on one route no longer cancels every stop
Result: 18 schools, about 1,490 students, 324 school stops a year

Slide 6: Route Eighteen Budget: $148,000
Used high-roof cargo van: $74,000
Refit (shelving, wheelchair lift, inverter, mobile hotspot): $18,500
Opening collection for four new schools (2,400 books): $21,600
Added driver-librarian hours, 0.5 FTE, year one: $26,400
Driver training, vehicle signage, launch visits: $3,500
Contingency: $4,000
Total (one-time costs plus first-year added operating cost): $148,000

Slide 7: Three Sources Fund the Full Cost
Corrow County Library District one-time capital award: $40,000 (committed)
Beaumont-Tully Rural Literacy Fund: $85,000 (request pending)
Spring 2027 donor campaign: $23,000 (planned)
Total: $148,000
Our request covers 57% of the project. The other 43% comes from county and community money
Ongoing operations are stable: the county contract and the Voss Family Foundation grant are renewed for FY2027, and the state grant runs through June 2027

Slide 8: Our Request and Timeline
We ask the Beaumont-Tully Rural Literacy Fund for $85,000 toward Route Eighteen
Full funding by March 2027: buy and refit the van in spring 2027
June 2027: summer stops begin on the north route
August 2027: full school service at 18 schools
FY2027 goals: miss no more than three stops, get benchmark data from all 14 current schools, and have the van running north-county summer stops by June 2027
Contact: Marisol Quennell, Executive Director, Quillmere Rolling Library, Vashti Bend

P2.text:
Quillmere Rolling Library
Board meeting notes, October 21, 2026, Vashti Bend Community Room

P3.text: Present: June Okafor-Reyes (board chair), Abner Whitlock (treasurer), Marisol Quennell (executive director), Pete Danforth (driver-librarian), Lila Ferrand (board member)

P5.text: Marisol reported that program officer Celeste Harrow at the Beaumont-Tully Rural Literacy Fund invited us to present Route Eighteen at their December 4 review. We will ask for $85,000 toward the $148,000 total. The county capital award of $40,000 is committed, and the spring donor campaign covers the last $23,000.

P6.text: June asked for a short slide deck to go with the presentation. Marisol will own it. Draft to the board by November 20, 2026, final to Celeste by November 27.

P7.text: Instructions the board agreed on for the deck:

P8.text:
1. Keep it to eight slides or fewer. Ms. Harrow said reviewers get ten minutes per applicant.
2. Open with the problem: 11 missed stops last year, all from the 2009 vehicle, and four north-county schools with 310 students waiting to join.
3. Show the full $148,000 budget line by line and all three funding sources, so the Fund sees that $85,000 is not the whole cost.
4. Abner insisted: the third-grade reading result (41 to 49 percent at six schools) goes in only with its caveat. Say plainly that the state tutors were in four of those schools and that we do not claim the gain. Do not round it into "raised reading scores."
5. Lila: no photos of children's faces and no student names. Ms. Akin's quote is fine because she gave permission.

P9.text: Pete will send updated stop counts if anything changes before November 20.

P12.text:
## FY2026 Annual Program Report (July 1, 2025 to June 30, 2026)
Quillmere Rolling Library is a two-person bookmobile nonprofit based in Vashti Bend. We carry a lending collection to rural elementary schools in Corrow County that have no school librarian and sit more than 25 miles from the nearest public library branch. This report covers our sixth fiscal year.

P13.text:
During the 2025-26 school year we served 14 elementary schools with a combined K-6 enrollment of 1,180 students. Each school got a visit every other week for 36 weeks, which put 252 school stops on the calendar. We also ran 40 summer stops at churches, a feed store parking lot, and the Corrow County fairgrounds, for a planned total of 292 stops.
We made 281 of those 292 stops. The 11 we missed were all caused by our vehicle, a 2009 bookmobile that crossed 214,000 miles this spring. It lost a transmission line in October, failed its brake inspection in February, and overheated twice in June. Each missed school stop means a class goes four weeks between visits, not two, and the teachers notice.
Key numbers for FY2026:

P14.text:
- Stops completed: 281 of 292 scheduled (96 percent)
- Items checked out: 21,460, up from 18,930 in FY2025
- Return rate: 91 percent
- New county library cards issued to students: 846
- Collection size at year end: 6,820 items
- Summer reading enrollment: 214 children; 131 finished the eight-book goal
- Teachers using our classroom crate loans: 52 of 61
The crate loans were new this year. A teacher picks a theme, such as weather or county history or chapter books for a reluctant fourth grade, and we leave a crate of 30 books in the classroom between visits. Fifty-two teachers used at least one crate. That accounts for about 4,100 of the year's checkouts, so a good share of our growth comes from this one change and not from more students walking up the steps.

P15.text: Six of our 14 schools agreed to share their spring reading benchmark results for third grade. At those six schools, the share of third graders reading at or above grade level rose from 41 percent in spring 2025 to 49 percent in spring 2026. That covers 188 students.
P15.locator: “One result, and what it does and does not show”

P16.text: We want to be plain about the limits. Six schools is not all 14, and the six that said yes may be the schools with the most engaged principals. We have no comparison group. And in the same year, the state funded a reading tutoring program that placed part-time tutors in four of those six schools. We cannot separate our effect from the tutors' effect, and we will not claim the eight-point gain as ours. What we can say is that the schools where children read the most books from our shelves were also the schools where reading scores went up. Next year we will ask all 14 schools for data and track checkouts per student so we can look at this more carefully.
P16.locator: “One result, and what it does and does not show”

P17.text: Dorrie Akin teaches third grade at Fallow Creek Elementary, one of our longest-serving stops. In May she wrote to us: "Bookmobile Tuesday is the only day the whole class runs to the window. When you missed in February, three kids asked me if you were coming back."

P18.text:
Total FY2026 expenses were $186,400.
| Line | Amount |
|---|---|
| Staff (1.5 FTE driver-librarians, 0.5 FTE coordinator) | $104,200 |
| Vehicle fuel, insurance, repairs and maintenance | $31,900 |
| Collection purchases and processing | $28,600 |
| Summer reading program | $6,300 |
| Administration, audit, software | $15,400 |
| Total | $186,400 |
Vehicle costs rose from $19,700 in FY2025 to $31,900 this year, almost all of it repairs. That jump is the clearest sign that the current vehicle is near the end of its working life.

P19.text:
Total FY2026 revenue was $191,250, leaving a small surplus of $4,850 that went to our operating reserve.
| Source | Amount |
|---|---|
| Corrow County Library District service contract | $78,000 |
| Harlan and Edie Voss Family Foundation (operating grant) | $45,000 |
| State Library rural services grant | $36,000 |
| Individual donors and the Friends of Quillmere | $22,750 |
| School participation fees | $9,500 |
| Total | $191,250 |
The county contract and the Voss grant are both renewed for FY2027 at the same amounts. The state grant is a two-year award that runs through June 2027.

P20.text:
Four more schools in the north end of the county, Dunmore, Pike Hollow, Sayer Flat and East Kettle, have asked to join. Together they enroll 310 K-6 students. None has a school librarian. We cannot add them with one aging vehicle that already misses stops.
Our plan for FY2027 is called Route Eighteen. We will buy a smaller second vehicle, a used high-roof cargo van refitted with shelving and a wheelchair lift, to run the north route. The 2009 bookmobile will stay in service on the shorter southern route through the end of FY2028 while we save for its replacement. Two vehicles also mean that a breakdown on one route no longer cancels every stop.
Route Eighteen budget (one-time costs plus first-year added operating cost):

P21.text:
| Line | Amount |
|---|---|
| Used high-roof cargo van | $74,000 |
| Refit: shelving, wheelchair lift, inverter, mobile hotspot | $18,500 |
| Opening collection for four new schools (2,400 books) | $21,600 |
| Added driver-librarian hours, 0.5 FTE, year one | $26,400 |
| Driver training, vehicle signage, launch visits | $3,500 |
| Contingency | $4,000 |
| Total | $148,000 |
How we will pay for it:
| Source | Amount | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Corrow County Library District one-time capital award | $40,000 | Committed |
| Beaumont-Tully Rural Literacy Fund | $85,000 | Request pending |
| Spring 2027 donor campaign | $23,000 | Planned |
| Total | $148,000 | |

P22.text: If Route Eighteen is fully funded by March 2027, the van will be bought and refitted in spring, run summer stops on the north route in June 2027, and start full school service in August 2027. At that point we expect to serve 18 schools and about 1,490 students with 324 school stops a year.

P23.text:
Our goals for FY2027 are simple: miss no more than three stops, get benchmark data from all 14 current schools, and have the Route Eighteen van running north-county summer stops by June 2027.
Marisol Quennell, Executive Director
Quillmere Rolling Library, Vashti Bend
